entry.title: Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1602
entry.content:
The Federal Court reviewed a Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of Mr Roseingrave’s visa cancellation. The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. The third ground concerning asserted Torres Strait ties failed.

Key holding: The limits of the primary considerations in Direction 110 do not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by a visa cancellation review applicant.

The correct identification of the limits of the primary considerations referred to in Direction 110 did not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by Mr Roseingrave.

entry.title: Application by Birrang Enterprise Development Co Ltd [2026] FWC 4167
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered Birrang’s application under s 120 of the Fair Work Act 2009 to reduce Mr Reid’s redundancy pay because it had offered him redeployment into a Support Coordinator role. Mr Reid declined the role but consented to the application. The Commission reduced his redundancy entitlement from four weeks to three weeks’ pay.

Key holding: Under s 120(1)(b)(i), whether alternative employment is acceptable is assessed objectively by the Commission, not by the employee’s subjective view, and if the preconditions are met the Commission has a broad discretion under s 120(2) to reduce redundancy pay.

Whether the alternative employment is "acceptable" is to be determined objectively, not by reference to whether Mr Reid considered that it was subjectively acceptable. The determination of whether alternative employment is acceptable requires me to make an assessment and value judgment.

entry.title: Ms Diane Hamilton v EDMI Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4187

She filed 82 days out of time and sought an extension under s 366(1) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The Fair Work Commission refused the extension and dismissed the application.

entry.title: Estefania Asensio Tato v Lycée Condorcet Trading AS The International French School Of Sydney Ltd [2026] FWC 4154
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dealt with a s 739 dispute brought by a former secondary Spanish teacher against her former school over alleged underpayments/classification for February and March 2025 work. The Commission upheld the school’s jurisdictional objection because the dispute was not raised until after employment ended, dismissed the application, and noted any underpayment claim could be pursued in court. The deed of release was not determinative.

Key holding: Under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission lacks jurisdiction to determine an enterprise agreement dispute where the dispute is raised after the employment relationship has ended.

The entitlements conferred in the Agreement remain enforceable for a limited period on application to the relevant Court, but the Commission is unable to deal with the dispute under the dispute resolution clause where the dispute was raised after the employment relationship had ended.

entry.title: Ms Joy Bultman v The Trustee For Scrappy's Metal Recycling Trust [2026] FWC 4149
entry.content:

Deputy President Bell dismissed the application for want of prosecution and no reasonable prospects of success in Bultman v The Trustee For Scrappy’s Metal Recycling Trust [2026] FWC 4149.

entry.title: Application by dnata Airport Services Pty Ltd Trading AS dnata [2026] FWC 4178
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered whether to approve dnata’s Queensland passenger services enterprise agreement [2026] FWC 4178. The TWU opposed approval, arguing the Agreement did not pass the better off overall test (BOOT), particularly regarding part-time shiftworker overtime and pay rates that might fall below the Award. The Commission largely accepted dnata’s Award construction and BOOT approach, but required further information or an undertaking about part-time day workers before approval.

Key holding: The BOOT is assessed at the test time, and the Commission does not speculate about future unknown Award wage outcomes when deciding whether employees are better off overall.

I accept the Applicant 's submission to the effect that it is not for the Commission to speculate about potential future unknown wage outcomes in assessing the BOOT, and that the BOOT is to be applied at test time.

entry.title: Ms Karen McClear v A Team Tuition Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4174
entry.content:
Ms McClear resigned after a lengthy suspension pending an unresolved misconduct investigation and brought a s 365 general protections claim alleging she was forced to resign. A Team Tuition objected that she was not dismissed within s 386. The Commission dismissed the application, finding she was not forced to resign because of the employer’s conduct and was therefore not dismissed.

Key holding: A resignation is a dismissal under s 386(1)(b) only where an objective assessment of the employer’s conduct shows it made resignation the probable result or left the employee with no effective or real choice but to resign.

In making that assessment, it is appropriate to make an objective analysis of the Respondent's conduct to determine whether it was of such a nature that resignation was the probable result or that the employee had no effective or real choice but to resign.

entry.content:

The Commission found her employment was terminated on 16 September 2026 after an earlier 30 June 2026 termination notice was withdrawn by consent, so the 7 September 2026 application was premature. Key holding: The Commission may decline to waive the irregularity in a premature unfair dismissal application where the applicant had a clear opportunity to withdraw and file a new application within time but did not do so.

The issue was whether Easter Saturday and Easter Sunday, both falling on a weekend, entitled employees to public holidays on the next two working days or only the next working day. entry.title: Fred-Tutavaha v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1586
entry.content:
The applicant, a New Zealand citizen who arrived in Australia aged four, sought judicial review of the Assistant Minister's decision under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to set aside an AAT decision revoking the cancellation of his visa. He ran three grounds — unreasonable delay, failure to consider immigration detention as a legal consequence, and legal unreasonableness in giving legal consequences "neutral weight" — with the Court also considering a proposed fourth ground on the national interest assessment.

Key holding: A failure to refer expressly to immigration detention in reasons for a s 501BA cancellation does not permit an inference that this legal consequence was not considered, where detention pending removal is an obvious and well-known statutory consequence and there is no barrier to removal.

It does not follow, however, that the proper inference is that the Assistant Minister failed to appreciate that a legal consequence of his decision was that the Applicant would be taken into immigration detention. The statement of reasons must be read fairly and as a whole, and the fact that a matter is not mentioned expressly does not necessarily mean it was not considered

The Commission held that "average weekly earnings" in clause 42 is to be worked out by reference to the Victorian workers' compensation concept of pre-injury average weekly earnings under the WIRC Act, and left the arithmetic to the parties.

Key holding: Where an enterprise agreement requires a top-up to 100% of "average weekly earnings" but does not define the term, that expression is to be calculated by reference to the pre-injury average weekly earnings concept in the Victorian workers' compensation legislation, with either s.153(1) or s.153(2) of the WIRC Act available.

entry.title: Application by UGL Operations and Maintenance Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4155
entry.content:
UGL Operations and Maintenance Pty Ltd applied to terminate a project-specific enterprise agreement after its nominal expiry date on the basis that it no longer covered any employees. entry.title: Application by Abdul Samee Paracha [2026] FWC 4142
entry.content:

entry.title: Mr Adrian Clay v Peninsula Directional Drilling Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4077
entry.content:
In [2026] FWC 4077, the Fair Work Commission considered a jurisdictional objection to Mr Adrian Clay’s unfair dismissal application against Peninsula Directional Drilling Pty Ltd. Mr Clay was General Manager with guaranteed annual earnings of $235,000, above the high-income threshold, and the Commission found he was not covered by the Clerks—Private Sector Award 2020 because his principal purpose was managing the business, not clerical work. The unfair dismissal application was dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

Key holding: Coverage under the Clerks—Private Sector Award 2020 requires the employee to be wholly or principally engaged in clerical work; incidental clerical duties do not establish coverage where the principal purpose of the role is management.

Having regard to the evidence of the duties and responsibilities of the work performed by Mr Clay, the extent to which he engaged in any clerical work as defined in the Award, was incidental. While I accept that some of the work performed by Mr Clay was clerical in nature, I am satisfied that he was not wholly or principally engaged in clerical work.

entry.title: Mr Josateki Vunimasi & Mr Aminio Cava and Others v Woodward Foods Australia Pty Ltd & Mr Richard Tomasevic [2026] FWCFB 284
entry.content:
This was a Full Bench appeal concerning seven PALM scheme workers whose s 365 general protections dismissal applications named Woodward Foods as respondent, although their actual employer/dismisser was Whales. The Deputy President found no valid s 365 application because they did not allege dismissal in contravention of Part 3-1, and the Full Bench refused permission to appeal. The appeal also sought to raise joint employment and host-employer oral promise arguments not argued at first instance.

Key holding: For a valid s 365 application, the person must have been dismissed and must allege that the dismissal contravened Part 3-1; otherwise the Commission’s s 368 powers are not enlivened.

It is abundantly clear that the Deputy President applied the principle outlined in Milford. He properly determined that the Appellants were not entitled to make applications under s 365 and nor were the functions of the Commission under s 368 enlivened because the second criterion was not met.
